https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/08.subtitle: Adopting ‘powerful posture’ means people can rival better-looking colleagues for non-verbal presence, say scientists
https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/2021/08.text:
Less attractive people should adopt a "powerful posture" at work to compensate for the inherent bias of employers towards good-looking workers, a new study suggests.
Previous research has found that life in the workplace is harder for less attractive people because they are less likely to be hired, earn less money and get worse appraisals from managers.
But scientists from the University of Buffalo, in the US, found that they can remedy the situation by using a power stance –a pose that involves a person having their feet shoulder-width apart, with hands on hips, chest out and chin up – to match beautiful colleagues for non-verbal presence.
The study, published in the journal Personnel Psychology, saw mock job interviews carried out with 300 participants and ranked each person on attractiveness and how hireable they were.
"In two experimental studies with data from 300 video interview pitches, we found that attractive individuals had a greater sense of power than their less attractive counterparts and thus exhibited a more effective non-verbal presence, which led to higher managerial ratings of their hireability," the researchers wrote.
Dr Min-Hsuan Tu, the study author, said: "We wanted to examine whether there's an overall bias toward beauty on the job, or if attractive people excel professionally because they're more effective communicators.
"What we found was that while good-looking people have a greater sense of power and are better non-verbal communicators, their less attractive peers can level the playing field during the hiring process by adopting a powerful posture.
"By adopting the physical postures associated with feelings of power and confidence, less attractive people can minimise behavioral differences in the job search.
"But power posing is not the only solution – anything that can make you feel more powerful, like doing a confidence self-talk, visualising yourself succeeding, or reflecting on past accomplishments before a social evaluation situation, can also help."
The power stance, or variations of it, has been common in politics for several years, with several high-profile members of the Conservative Party having been advocates of the technique.
Images from that time show Theresa May, George Osborne, Sajid Javid and David Cameron in the wide-based stance, but with their arms hanging by their sides rather than on their hips.
